name: Timberwolf
lede: Timberwolf is a pale, faintly warm grey named for the grey coat of the timber wolf rather than any pigment or dye.

sections.title: A wolf's grey coat
sections.body:
Our library traces the name to a Wikipedia color list, which gives no date for when the name entered use [1]. The word points to the animal's fur rather than a material, place or person [1].

Its nearest named neighbor is [[light-grey]], 3.0 units of CIEDE2000 away and described as almost the same [2]. [[platinum]] sits at 3.4, lighter, [[grey-white]] at 4.1, almost the same, and [[papyrus-white]] at 4.4, also almost the same [2]. Measured in LCH it reads lightness 86, chroma 3, among the palest, least saturated colors in our library [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this color in 642 of 23,781 paintings (2.7 percent), more common than 80 percent of the named colors, as photographed [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 61 of 1,674 paintings from that century, 1.7 times the expected rate [3]. Carlos de Haes is its most devoted painter, using it in 5 of 29 of his works in our archive, 4.7 times the baseline of the museums those works come from [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, a role measured by lightness rank within the canvas, in 77 percent of matched works [3]. It shares canvases with [[cool-grey]] and Light Mouse Grey well above chance [3]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [3].
